source.title: Almost Free State Prediction Separation
source.authors: John Langford; Nathan Godey; Giovanni Monea; Yoav Artzi; Harry Dong; Ying Fan; Gustavo H. de Rosa; Zheng Zhan

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a pretraining-loss improvement is accompanied by downstream improvements, using downstream metrics rather than a scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates downstream metrics for pause-training variants alongside a matched control, bearing on V6. It does not fit power laws, test extrapolation, sweep model size or compute to find an optimal allocation, or test architecture-shape sensitivity. Its results about loss and training cost alone do not establish those versions.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper on free pause tokens at a single 1B scale. It cites the link between loss and capability as motivation. Its downstream section asks whether its own method's CE gain carries over to downstream metrics, comparing method variants with a matched control. It fits no power law and does not sweep parameters, tokens or compute. It does not test whether downstream performance tracks scale or loss predictably. It uses a two-point token-scaling slope (~0.037 nats/doubling) as a tool to build iso-compute baselines, including a short extrapolation to 157B, without testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors conclude that their free-pause method gives a modest iso-token and iso-parameter gain at 1B scale. Its training overhead falls from ~1.9× FLOPs to 1.33× wall-clock (as low as 1.09×), with free inference. At iso-node-hours every variant beats the control (−0.005 to −0.013 nats). At strict iso-FLOP the full pause turns slightly negative (+0.006). The downstream gain (CORE 0.327 to 0.347 iso-token; matching the 150B control iso-compute) shows the improvement is not loss-only.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architectural and training-cost study of free-pause state–prediction separation, not a scaling-law fit or a reproduction of the original scaling-law methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes are reported for full pause and two phase-switch schedules, at 100B tokens; comparisons distinguish iso-token from iso-compute.
record.problems: The study is limited to a single 1B scale and a single primary seed. Individual lm-eval task scores are within their 95% confidence intervals and are not shown; downstream results are aggregate measures with reported standard errors.

untested.parts: No power-law fits or sweeps over parameters, tokens or compute. The 0.037 nats/doubling slope comes from two control endpoints.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs. The 157B baseline is a short two-point extrapolation used as a tool.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested for power-law form.
There is no relationship between scale or loss and downstream performance across scales. Downstream metrics are reported only to check the method's gain, at one 1B scale.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' on V6 conflates 'our method's loss gain shows up downstream' with V6's claim that downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. All rows are method-vs-control or control references, so they are relinked to none. The only scale-like contrast is control 100B vs 150B tokens (CE 2.8957 to 2.8742; CORE 0.327 to 0.348). It is two points at one model size and is used as the iso-compute reference, so it is too thin to count as a V6 test. Single scale, single primary seed.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted growth trends.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law form across modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
Tests downstream outcomes for loss-improving variants at one model scale, not a predictive relationship across scales or a range of pretraining losses.
No comparison of scaling-law fitting choices, exponents, or curve shapes.
